title: Structural typing and excess property checking
markdown:
## Why this matters

TypeScript's structural system is not "duck typing with annotations." Excess property checking and assignability rules explain surprising errors at API boundaries.

## The simple version

Forget class names entirely and think of TypeScript as checking whether one key ring opens the same doors as another key ring. If key ring A opens every door that key ring B needs opened (and maybe a few more), A can stand in for B, it doesn't matter what the key rings are called or where they came from. That's structural typing: shape, not name, decides compatibility.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["interface Point {x, y}"] -.same shape.-> B["interface Coord {x, y}"]
  B == assignable both ways ==> A
  C["literal {x: 1, y: 2, z: 3}"] -- "extra key z" --> D{"Fresh literal?"}
  D -- yes --> E[Excess property error]
  D -- no, came through a variable --> F[Allowed]
```

Where the analogy breaks: with real keys, having an extra key on the ring never hurts. TypeScript disagrees, but *only* when you hand over a freshly-written object literal directly. Pass that same "extra key" through a variable first, and TypeScript stops checking for extras, because it assumes a variable might reasonably be reused elsewhere with a wider shape. The excess-property check exists specifically to catch typos on literals (`{ nmae: 'x' }`), not to enforce that shapes are ever exact.

## Core mechanics

Types are compared by shape. Fresh object literals get excess property checks; variables widened through aliases do not. Optional vs `undefined` positions matter for `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.

## Mental model

Think "compatibility of required members," not nominal names. Two interfaces with the same fields are interchangeable even if declared separately.

## Runnable experiment

```ts
function takesId(x: { id: string }) {}

takesId({ id: '1', extra: true }); // error: excess property 'extra'

const withExtra = { id: '1', extra: true };
takesId(withExtra); // OK: went through a variable first, no fresh-literal check
```

## Trade-offs and failure modes

Teams sometimes "fix" an excess property error by routing a literal through a throwaway variable, silencing a real typo instead of catching it. The check exists to catch exactly that mistake, bypass it deliberately, not by accident.

## Tool-building exercise

Sketch a small CLI that prints assignability failures by driving the compiler API on two type nodes.

## Key takeaways

- Shapes compare, names do not.
- Fresh literals are checked strictly.
- Optional properties are not the same as `undefined` unions without `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.

exercise.title: Break and fix an excess-property error
exercise.instructions:
Write a function that accepts `{ id: string; role: 'admin' | 'user' }`. Call it three ways: a fresh object literal with a typo, the same value assigned to a wider variable first, and a literal checked with `satisfies`. Add a fourth case that compares `role?: Role` with `role: Role | undefined` under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.

Acceptance criteria: keep the expected errors visible with `@ts-expect-error`; explain why the variable path allows an extra key; show that `satisfies` catches the typo without widening valid literals; distinguish absent from present-undefined at runtime; and define the public API shape you would choose.
exercise.deliverable: Four compiler-checked cases plus a short boundary-design note explaining structural compatibility, fresh-literal checking, `satisfies`, and optional-property semantics.
hints: Use `@ts-expect-error` for intentional negative cases so CI proves the error still exists.
`satisfies` deliberately re-enables the fresh-literal check even though you're assigning to a plain variable, which is exactly why it exists.
The compiler doesn't track 'this variable came from a literal with an extra field' once it's been assigned, widening erases that history.

questions.prompt: When does excess property checking apply?
choices: Fresh object literals assigned to a typed target
questions.correct_answer: Fresh object literals assigned to a typed target
questions.explanation: The misconception: assuming TypeScript always enforces exact shapes. It only checks fresh literals, like the key-ring analogy, an extra key is fine once it's on a keyring (variable) you're handing over, but flagged the moment you're cutting a brand new key on the spot.
questions.learning_objective: excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals

questions.prompt: Are two interfaces with identical fields mutually assignable?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, TypeScript compares structure, not declaration name, so identical shapes are assignable barring branded/nominal tricks.
questions.explanation: The misconception: expecting class-like nominal typing, where the declared name matters. TypeScript checks whether the 'key ring' opens the same doors, identical shape means interchangeable, regardless of the interface's name.
questions.learning_objective: structural compatibility ignores declared type names

questions.prompt: What breaks assignability first when adding an unknown key to a literal?
questions.explanation: The misconception: assuming a superset shape is always fine since it 'has everything required.' The excess-property check specifically targets unknown keys on fresh literals to catch typos, independent of whether the required fields are all present.
questions.learning_objective: unknown keys on fresh literals fail even when required fields are present

questions.prompt: With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` enabled, which value satisfies `{ theme?: 'dark' | 'light' }`?
questions.explanation: The misconception is treating absence and present-with-undefined as identical. Under exact optional properties, `theme?: T` permits the key to be absent; assigning undefined requires `undefined` to appear explicitly in T.
questions.learning_objective: distinguish optional property absence from an explicit undefined value

questions.prompt: You are publishing a component prop type used by many teams. Explain when a structural interface is enough and when you would add a brand or runtime validation.
questions.correct_answer: Use a plain structural type when any value with the required shape is valid. Add a brand when accidentally mixing structurally identical domain values would be dangerous, and validate at runtime whenever the value crosses an untrusted boundary because TypeScript types disappear after compilation.
questions.explanation: The misconception is asking the static type system to prove runtime trust or domain identity automatically. Structural typing is convenient inside trusted code, while brands and validators solve different boundary risks.
questions.learning_objective: choose structural types, brands, and runtime validators according to boundary risk
